Article Title: Made-in-India 5G Radio Moves Closer To Market, Bulk Supplies Expected In 2027
Article Text:
Prof Kiran Kumar Kuchi, IIT Hyderabad; Prof Debabrata Das, Director, IIIT-Bangalore and Sridhar Pillalamarri, CEO, IIITB COMET Foundation (L-R), showcasing Made-in-India 5G and 5G-Advanced technology.

Bengaluru: A Made-in-India 5G radio has taken a step towards commercial deployment, with deep-tech company WiSig Networks opening commercial orders for the technology. Bulk supplies are expected to begin in 2027.The development is significant for India’s efforts to reduce dependence on imported telecom equipment and build capabilities in advanced wireless communication. The technology, which also has applications in 5G-Advanced networks, emerged from research led by Prof Kiran Kuchi at IIT Hyderabad, with support from IIITB COMET Foundation, Bengaluru, under the Department of Science and Technology’s National Mission on Interdisciplinary Cyber-Physical Systems (NM-ICPS).The 5G radio uses multiple antennas working together to transmit and receive several signals simultaneously, a technique that helps improve network capacity, performance and coverage. Such capabilities are increasingly important as mobile data consumption rises and networks need to handle more connected devices and higher data traffic.The research was licensed to WiSig Networks, a deep-tech company founded at IIT Hyderabad.The company first showcased the radio at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona in March 2026 and subsequently opened commercial orders at the India Mobile Congress in New Delhi in October.Prof. Debabrata Das, chairman of the governing body of IIITB COMET Foundation and director of IIIT-Bangalore, said the development demonstrated how academic research could progress towards commercial products.“This is precisely the kind of outcome that research funding should aim to achieve. It is encouraging to see research undertaken at an academic institution, with support from IIITB COMET Foundation, progress towards a product that has the potential for commercial deployment,” he said, underlining the importance of academia-industry collaboration in building indigenous capabilities in emerging technologies.Sridhar Pillalamarri, CEO of IIITB COMET Foundation, said: “The real value of research is also reflected in its ability to address practical needs.” He said the development showed how research support, technology transfer and industry participation could bring indigenous innovations closer to the market.The Foundation, established at IIIT-Bangalore under the NM-ICPS programme, supports research and technology development in advanced communication systems, including indigenous solutions for 5G and next-generation networks.The opening of commercial orders marks an important stage in the development of the technology, although large-scale supplies are yet to begin. Its commercial deployment will be an indicator of how effectively Indian research and industry can work together to build and take advanced telecommunications products to market.
Article Summary: WiSig Networks opens commercial orders for the technology. Bulk supplies are expected to begin in 2027. Development is significant for India’s efforts to reduce dependence on imported telecom equipment. Technology emerged from research led by Prof Kiran Kuchi at IIT Hyderabad.

NEW DELHI: The government is planning to convene a special session of Parliament to secure the passage of a Constitution amendment bill linked to the implementation of women's reservation, PTI reported.According to the report, the BJP-led Centre is confident of securing 15 to 18 votes more than the 361 required to achieve a two-thirds majority and pass the proposed legislation. However, the dates and duration of the proposed special session remain unclear.The possibility of convening Parliament at short notice remains open, as the Monsoon Session, during which both Houses were adjourned sine die (indefinitely) on August 13, has yet to be prorogued. The session has now remained unprorogued for 91 days, surpassing the previous record of 87 days set in 2008.While an extended sitting of an existing session requires a minimum notice of two days, convening a fresh session requires at least 14 days' notice.The government's decision to keep the Monsoon Session unprorogued has consequently triggered speculation about the possibility of an extended sitting or a special session to consider the proposed amendment.The Constitution does not specify any timeframe within which a House must be prorogued after being adjourned sine die. Nor does keeping a session in continuation without formally proroguing it for an extended period, by itself, constitute any constitutional or procedural impropriety.The proposed constitutional amendment seeks to increase the strength of the Lok Sabha from the existing 543 seats to a maximum of 850 through delimitation, paving the way for the implementation of 33% reservation for women in Parliament and state legislative assemblies.The move follows the failure of a similar Constitution amendment bill to secure the required majority in the Lok Sabha during a special sitting of the Budget Session on April 17.The government is proposing a 50% increase in Lok Sabha seats for every state to address concerns raised by southern states, as it seeks to implement the women's reservation law before the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.A fresh draft, which builds on the earlier bill, is understood to propose retaining the existing proportion of seats among states based on the 1971 Census.However, this is among several proposals under consideration, and no final decision has been taken, according to government sources.
Article Summary: The Centre is reportedly confident of securing 15-18 more votes than the 361 required to achieve a two-thirds majority and pass the proposed legislation. The dates and duration of the proposed special session remain unclear. The possibility of convening Parliament at short notice remains open, as the Monsoon Session has yet to be prorogued.

Article Title: India simplifies visa rules: Categories cut to 9 from 13, application fields reduced by up to 70%
Article Text:
The rationalisation of visitor visa, earlier called tourist visa, allows flexibility for short and long stays.

NEW DELHI: Having simplified its visa regime by cutting the total visa categories to 9 from 13 and sub-categories to 23 from 49 and also reducing the information sought from foreign applicants across all 23 sub-categories, the ministry of home affairs (MHA) will be MHA updating its IT systems by year-end, to grant visas per new rationalisation."The step aims at making it (visa regime) more compact, coherent and responsive to the requirements of foreign nationals visiting India," the home ministry said in a statement on Wednesday. As part of the revamp, the main visa categories were first cut on 22 to 13 and sub-categories to 49 from 63 in October last year, and further to 9 and 23 respectively on August 27 this year. This simplification was done after studying the visa system followed by the developed countries as well as the global standards."The consolidation of similar purposes of travel is aimed at providing greater clarity and ease in identifying the appropriate visa category while facilitating legitimate foreign arrivals," said a ministry spokesperson.Currently electronic visa or e visa is processed by electronic travel authorization under 13 sub categories. The e-visa facility is available to nationals of 172 countries.The MHA has also made visa application simpler, cutting the fields/columns by upto 70% across all 23 sub-categories of visas."The initiative aims to significantly reduce the information required from foreign nationals, while retaining essential details necessary for visa processing. This will reduce time and effort required to complete the application and also enhance administrative efficiency by facilitating more focused scrutiny and processing of visa application," said MHA.The rationalisation of visitor visa, earlier called tourist visa, allows flexibility for short and long stays. The name visitor visa reflects a broader range of permitted purposes beyond conventional tourism. The category has been organised into two sub-categories, V-1 and V-2. V-1 covers short-term activities such as business meetings, medical consultations, wellness retreats, and short term courses. It is granted for 30 days with multiple entries. V2 is for longer-duration visits, with validity of 1, 5 or 10 years, as specified.The medical visa framework retains separate provisions for treatment under conventional and AYUSH systems. M-1 Visa covers medical treatment other than treatment under AYUSH systems, while M-3 Visa covers treatment under AYUSH systems. M-1 and M-3 Visas, including their e-Visa variants, will be granted for one year as a default option with multiple entries.This arrangement gives patients greater predictability when treatment involves multiple consultations, follow-up appointments or staged procedures.In the student visa category, S-1 covers school and college education while the S-2 is meant for PhD and research scholars in Indian universities.Business visas shall now also divided into B-1 and B-2. B-1 Visa covers long-term, licence-based business activities, including foreign nationals seeking to establish industrial or business ventures in India. B-2 Visa covers short-term, contract-based business activities, including Production Investment Business, conferences, sports, performative arts and films.A specific provision has also been made for foreign subject-matter specialists, engineers and technical personnel engaged by Indian companies. Such personnel may be granted a production investment business visa under the B-2 category through the e-Visa platform. This was earlier granted under e-B4 visa nomenclature."This differentiation gives businesses greater clarity when planning long-term investments as against short-term contractual assignments. The dedicated provision for technical specialists can facilitate timely deployment of expertise for setting up and operationalising industrial facilities, transferring technology, etc," as per MHA.The ministry said the changes in visa regime reduce overlap between visa categories and make the framework easier to navigate for visitors, patients, students, researchers, investors and business professionals. The rationalisation is intended to support legitimate travel, education, healthcare and economic engagement with India through clearer, purpose-based visa options, subject to applicable eligibility criteria and conditions.
Article Summary: Ministry of home affairs (MHA) will be MHA updating its IT systems by year-end, to grant visas per new rationalisation. The rationalisation of visitor visa, earlier called tourist visa, allows flexibility for short and long stays. The name visitor visa reflects a broader range of permitted purposes beyond conventional tourism.

Article Title: Sheikh Hasina, water and trade: Roadblocks in India-Bangladesh ties
Article Text:
The Sheikh Hasina question: At the heart of diplomatic tension

Sheikh Hasina's road back to Bangladesh

Shared rivers, competing interest

The road ahead for India-Bangladesh ties

Over two years ago, student protests against the quota system in Bangladesh’s government jobs evolved into a nationwide uprising that brought down the government of then Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina , forcing her to flee to India. The political upheaval ushered in a period of considerable strain in bilateral relations with India, and New Delhi-Dhaka ties have since deteriorated significantly. This is reflected in the fact that Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, who assumed office in February, is yet to visit New Delhi, despite having travelled to other countries in the region.The tensions have also spilled over into negotiations on the future of the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty and bilateral trade. Political mistrust has complicated efforts to reach a consensus on water-sharing, while reciprocal trade restrictions have added to economic friction.These issues have emerged as significant roadblocks in bilateral ties. The challenge for New Delhi and Dhaka, therefore, is not merely to resolve disagreements but to ensure that political differences do not undermine the broader framework of bilateral cooperation.The departure of Sheikh Hasina from Bangladesh in August 2024 marked a turning point in bilateral ties. Her subsequent presence in India became a major source of disagreement between New Delhi and Dhaka.During her tenure, Sheikh Hasina had maintained close relations with successive governments in New Delhi, cooperating on issues such as counterterrorism, connectivity, transit and regional security. India, in turn, viewed her as an important partner in maintaining stability in its eastern neighbourhood.However, this fuelled perceptions among a significant section of the public in Bangladesh that India had prioritised its own strategic interests over broader democratic and political concerns in their country. This perception contributed to a growing anti-India sentiment and played a part in the political developments that eventually led to Sheikh Hasina’s ouster.Since then, both the Muhammad Yunus-led interim administration that succeeded Sheikh Hasina and the subsequent Bangladesh Nationalist Party government, elected in February, have repeatedly sought the former prime minister’s extradition to face the law for “crimes against humanity” linked to the July Uprising, as the movement is known as in Bangladesh. Meanwhile, India has maintained that the request is being examined through the established legal process.Also, Sheikh Hasina has already announced that she would return to Bangladesh in December, a timeline that is now drawing closer. If her return materialises, it could bring the extradition question to a close, although the legal and political issues surrounding her return may continue to test ties. A press conference she addressed on August 5, the second anniversary of her resignation, further complicated matters.According to Sreeradha Datta, Professor of International Affairs at OP Jindal Global University, the extradition impasse is not a roadblock in itself; rather, it is the manner in which the two sides have handled the issue that has become the stumbling block.“The roadblock is how the two sides deal with it. And the fact that the Bangladesh government laid down a condition like that (extradition) for a visit to occur is actually what has complicated the matter,” she said, referring to Tarique Rahman’s yet-to-take-place visit.Datta added that Rahman could have visited India and discussed the matter with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, but setting a precondition only complicated the issue further.Ultimately, how the Sheikh Hasina matter is handled will be an important test of New Delhi and Dhaka’s ability to manage political differences while keeping the broader relationship on track.While the extradition impasse represents a relatively recent political challenge, disagreements over river water-sharing have long been a feature of India-Bangladesh relations. Since they share 54 transboundary rivers, differences over the equitable distribution of water are natural.However, a formal water-sharing treaty exists only for the river known as the Ganga in India and the Padma in Bangladesh. Signed on December 12, 1996, the 30-year agreement is due to expire on December 12 this year. With the renewal deadline approaching, Dhaka has called for a new or revised, longer-term agreement that includes a “guarantee” clause to ensure an assured supply of water to Bangladesh, particularly during the dry season and periods of low river levels.Datta noted that water remains an emotive and sensitive issue for Bangladesh, adding that while a new 30-year agreement may or may not materialise, she hoped the two sides could reach an interim arrangement.“For Bangladesh, water is the most emotive and sensitive issue. … Even if we don't expect a long-term 30-year agreement, I hope there is an interim agreement because both are agro-based economies and Bangladesh’s dependence on the common rivers is far more,” she said.Beyond the Ganga/Padma, India and Bangladesh have also had longstanding disagreements over the sharing of Teesta waters. A deal came close to being finalised in 2011 but was blocked by then West Bengal chief minister Mamata Banerjee, citing her state’s needs. Dhaka has been seeking a formal treaty to secure an adequate share of Teesta’s waters, particularly during the dry season, when declining flows affect irrigation and agricultural activities.With the BJP, which has been India’s governing party since 2014, now also governing West Bengal, there are hopes that the long-pending Teesta agreement may finally materialise.Nevertheless, against the backdrop of recent tensions, the unresolved water-sharing disputes remain another major irritant in India-Bangladesh ties.Despite strained ties, India remains Bangladesh’s third-largest trading partner. It briefly overtook the United States in February before Washington reclaimed the second spot, while China continues to be the largest trading partner by a distance.Yet, with both sides imposing trade restrictions, economic ties remain under strain, adding another layer of friction to an already tense relationship.For instance, in April 2025, Dhaka restricted the entry of Indian yarn through several land ports, citing concerns over its domestic textile industry. The same month, New Delhi withdrew the transshipment facility that had allowed Bangladeshi export cargo to pass through Indian territory en route to third countries. The following month, India further tightened import restrictions on several categories of Bangladeshi goods through land ports, including ready-made garments and certain processed products.The curbs were discussed during trade negotiations held in New Delhi last month, marking the first meeting of the bilateral joint working group after a prolonged gap. The Bangladeshi side reportedly called for a review of restrictions on the entry of goods through Indian land ports, while India sought the removal of curbs on its cotton yarn exports.Both sides also called for the removal of other trade restrictions imposed by the other.Despite continued engagement through bilateral talks, these differences remain unresolved, adding to the wider set of contentious issues straining ties between New Delhi and Dhaka.Likely anticipating Tarique Rahman's eventual rise to power, New Delhi began reaching out to him following his return to Bangladesh in December 2025, after a 17-year stay in the UK. External affairs minister S Jaishankar attended the funeral of former Bangladesh Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, Rahman’s mother, who passed away just days after her son’s return to the country. Later, Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and foreign secretary Vikram Misri represented India at Rahman’s swearing-in ceremony.Then, in April, former Union minister Dinesh Trivedi was appointed as India’s high commissioner to Bangladesh, marking a relatively rare instance of a political figure being chosen for a diplomatic posting.According to Sreeradha Datta, the move signals New Delhi’s seriousness about improving ties with Bangladesh and has, therefore, been well-received in Dhaka.“He (Trivedi) has been able to have a good outreach and he seems to have got along well with the Bangladeshis. His appointment has been well received and it probably conveyed to Bangladesh that the government was giving more attention and hoping that a political appointee would have greater ability to move things,” she said.Having been in the post for only six months, whether Trivedi can help bring about a broader reset in the relationship remains to be seen.India-Bangladesh relationship remains strained by a range of unresolved issues, extending beyond the impasse over Sheikh Hasina’s extradition to disputes over river-water sharing and trade. These include concerns over India’s alleged “forced push-ins” of suspected undocumented Bangladeshi immigrants, the alleged killings of Bangladeshi “civilians” by the Border Security Force at the India-Bangladesh border, and Dhaka’s pro-Pakistan tilt that began under the interim administration, among others.Yet, the relationship remains strategically important for both sides: Bangladesh is critical to India’s security interests, while Dhaka depends on New Delhi across several key sectors.Against this backdrop, Datta stressed that cooperation between New Delhi and Dhaka is in the interest of both, as well as the wider region.“India and Bangladesh have to work together for their own benefit. For the last two years, we've seen them not work with each other (but) it makes greater sense for not only the bilateral partners, but also for the region when India and Bangladesh work together,” she said.Ultimately, despite the many unresolved roadblocks, India and Bangladesh have little choice but to find a way to work together because of geography and shared strategic interests. The question is how soon both sides can move beyond the current strains.
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina's extradition to India is at the heart of diplomatic tension. Tensions have spilled over into negotiations on the future of the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty and bilateral trade. Political mistrust has complicated efforts to reach a consensus on water-sharing. reciprocal trade restrictions have added to economic friction.

Article Title: UP polls: Owaisi, Azad likely to announce alliance on Nov 12
Article Text:
Owaisi and Chandrashekhar Azad are set to join hands ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections, seeking to consolidate Dalit and minority votes

NEW DELHI: All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen ( AIMIM ) chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Azad Samaj Party (Kanshiram) president Chandrashekhar Azad are likely to announce an alliance for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections at a joint press conference in Lucknow on Thursday, November 12.The proposed tie-up could mark an attempt by the two parties to build a political front outside the BJP-led NDA and the Samajwadi Party-Congress alliance. Both parties are looking to consolidate support among Dalit and minority voters, who together account for nearly 41 per cent of Uttar Pradesh's electorate, according to the figures cited by party leaders.AIMIM spokesperson Shadab Chauhan confirmed that the two parties would join hands, but said details of the agreement would be made public at the press conference, news agency PTI reported.The event is expected to be held at a hotel in Gomtinagar and will be addressed by Owaisi and leaders of the Bhim Army.Both leaders have reached Lucknow ahead of the announcement. Asked about the proposed alliance, Azad said its aim was to strengthen the position of young people, farmers and marginalised sections. He said further details would be shared on Thursday.The parties have not yet disclosed how many of the state's 403 assembly seats they intend to contest.It is also unclear whether other smaller parties will join the proposed front.The development follows Owaisi's unsuccessful attempt to secure a place in the INDIA bloc's seat-sharing arrangement in Uttar Pradesh. The AIMIM chief had set an October 2 deadline for the Samajwadi Party and Congress to respond to his offer, but neither party agreed to include him in the alliance.While AIMIM has a limited electoral footprint in Uttar Pradesh, Owaisi has influence among sections of the minority community. Azad, the Nagina MP, has been seeking to expand his support among young Dalit voters. Their proposed partnership could therefore add another political equation to the contest, as the BJP looks to retain power for a third consecutive term and the opposition seeks to challenge it.
Article Summary: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi and Azad Samaj Party (Kanshiram) president Chandrashekhar Azad are likely to announce an alliance for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections. The parties have not yet disclosed how many of the state's 403 assembly seats they intend to contest.

Article Title: Complete data could've raised average Diwali pollution level in Delhi by 49%
Article Text:
Complete data could've raised avg Diwali pollution level 49%

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Missing PM2.5 data from monitoring stations could have raised the city's average pollution level by 49% on Diwali, according to an analysis by Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).Had the missing readings been recorded at 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre (g/m³), the city's average PM2.5 level would have increased from 269 to 400(g/m³), it revealed. The daily national ambient air quality standard for PM2.5 is 60 g/m³ and WHO's safe guideline is 15 g/m³.The analysis was done a day after Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) said its stations' analysers were calibrated to measure particulate matter concentrations only up to 1,000g/m³ and could not display readings beyond it on Diwali night for several hours.Nor were these readings considered for calculating the average AQI, it said.CREA said if 400g/m³ had been considered, city's AQI on Monday would have risen from 344 (very poor) to near severe. AQI is calculated based on 8 pollutants, including PM2.5.TOI reported Tuesday that CPCB had stopped giving data on particulate matter at the peak of Diwali night pollution for several hours after particulate matter levels at air quality monitoring stations surpassed 1,000g/m³.However, Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC), which operates 43 of the total 60 stations, gave readings on Diwali night that crossed 1,000g/m³. At least at 11 locations, the hourly PM2.5 concentration was above 2,000g/m³. In four, it was above 3,000.CPCB compiles data from all 60 stations and releases the AQI. One station has been defunct for the past few months.The latest analysis examined hourly PM2.5 data from 59 monitoring stations between 4pm on Nov 8 and 4pm on Nov 9, corresponding to the 24-hour averaging period used for CPCB's 4pm AQI bulletin on Nov 9. It analysed 1,416 hours (24 hours x 59 stations).It found that 255 of the 1,416 expected station-hour observations or 18% were missing. CREA conducted a sensitivity analysis by assigning them a value of 1,000g/m³, the upper measurement limit cited by CPCB for particulate matter. Under this scenario, the pooled average PM2.5 concentration across the expected observations increased from 269g/m³ to 400g/m³, a rise of 49%."The peak PM2.5 levels of Delhi was 584 g/m³ at 1am on Nov 9 when there was missing data. However, after replacing the missing data with 1,000 g/m³, the peak PM2.5 concentration was 825 g/m³ at 2am and 824 g/m³ at 3am," said CREA.It clarified that the sensitivity analysis does not establish that all 255 missing observations were caused by PM2.5 concentrations exceeding 1,000g/m³. Assigning the upper measurement limit to these observations was only an illustrative exercise to understand how the reported average could change under such a scenario.TOI reported Tuesday that hourly PM2.5 levels at Mundka touched 3,744g/m³ at 2am Monday, according to DPCC's data. However, CPCB did not share Mundka's PM2.5 readings from 12 midnight to 4 am.
Article Summary: Missing PM2.5 data from monitoring stations could have raised the city's average pollution level by 49% on Diwali. Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) said its stations' analysers were calibrated to measure particulate matter only up to 1,000g/m³.

Article Title: Centre simplifies visa regime: Paperwork cut by 70%, categories reduced from 13 to 9
Article Text:
The changes were introduced on August 27, 2026

Student visa category

reorganised

NEW DELHI: The Centre has simplified India's visa regime, reducing the number of main visa categories from 13 to nine and sub-categories from 49 to 23, in a move aimed at making travel, education and medical treatment in the country easier for foreign nationals.The ministry of home affairs (MHA), in a press release on Wednesday, said the number of fields to be filled in visa application forms across all 23 sub-categories has been reduced by 65-70%, making the process easier, faster and more applicant-friendly.This follows an earlier rationalisation in October 2025, when the number of main visa categories was reduced from 22 to 13 and sub-categories from 63 to 49.As part of the changes, the Student Visa category has been consolidated into two broad sub-categories — S-1 and S-2.The S-1 Visa covers school, graduate and post-graduate education, while the S-2 Visa covers PhD scholars and research students in Indian universities, visiting faculty, foreign research students visiting India, scientific and anthropological expeditions, internships and exchange programmes, among other specified academic activities.Foreign students enrolled in Indian educational institutions through the Study in India portal may be granted an e-S1 Visa for up to five years or for the duration of their academic course, whichever is shorter.The visa will allow multiple entries.Under the revised framework, the erstwhile Tourist Visa has been renamed the Visitor Visa. Provisions relating to medical, student and business visas have also been reorganised.The MHA is updating its information technology systems to implement the revised framework, with visas under the new system expected to be issued by the end of 2026.
Article Summary: The number of main visa categories has been reduced from 13 to nine. The Student Visa category has been consolidated into two broad sub-categories. The erstwhile Tourist Visa has been renamed the Visitor Visa. Provisions relating to medical, student and business visas have been reorganised.

Article Title: Green energy push helped India save $100bn over last 15 yrs: IEA
Article Text:
Green energy push helped India save $100bn over last 15 yrs: IEA

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Expansion of renewable energy (RE) capacity over the past 15 years helped India save more than $100 billion in coal and natural gas import costs, the International Energy Agency (IEA) has said in a recent report.With 300GW of RE capacity, India has emerged as the world's second-fastest-growing renewables market, strengthening its energy security, the report said. India added 168GW of solar and 38GW of wind capacity between March 2014 and Sept 2026, while installed bioenergy capacity reached nearly 12GW. With RE capacity expected to reach 530GW by 2030, IEA estimated that cumulative savings on coal and natural gas imports could reach $240 billion by 2030, assuming international fuel prices remain broadly at their 2024-25 average levels. Annual savings are projected to reach around $35 billion by then, exceeding India's entire spending on non-coking coal and natural gas imports in FY25.The India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026 estimated that without the solar PV, wind and bioenergy capacity added since 2010, India's coal imports in 2025 would have been around 110 million tonnes higher."India's experience shows how consistent policies can help drive down renewable energy costs and attract investment, offering valuable lessons for other emerging economies," said IEA executive director Fatih Birol.India achieved its target of sourcing 50% of installed electricity capacity from non-fossil fuel sources in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.IEA said the growth extended beyond large plants, supported by rooftop solar installations, corporate RE procurement and expansion of domestic manufacturing facilities. It specifically highlighted the PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana for accelerating rooftop solar installations and PM-KUSUM for supporting solar-powered irrigation pumps and farm feeders.
Article Summary: Green energy push helped India save $100bn over last 15 yrs: IEA. With 300GW of RE capacity, India has emerged as the world's second-fastest-growing renewables market. India added 168GW of solar and 38GW of wind capacity between March 2014 and Sept 2026.

Article Title: 'Misleading': Election Commission rejects claims of vote-count discrepancies in 2024 polls
Article Text:
The poll body shared constituency-wise details to clarify the figures.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Wednesday rejected social media claims of discrepancies between the number of votes polled and votes counted in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections and state assembly polls describing the allegations as "misleading. "In a post on X, the poll body shared screenshots of claims concerning constituencies in Maharashtra, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir, along with constituency-wise data to clarify the figures."This is with reference to a social media post claiming inconsistencies in the number of votes polled and votes counted in the General Elections to the Lok Sabha, 2024 and General Elections to Legislative Assemblies of States held in 2024," the ECI said in a statement.The Commission said it publishes details of electors, votes polled through electronic voting machines (EVMs), postal ballots and total votes cast in its statistical reports and index cards. These records are available on its website.It also questioned the reference to "internal records" in the claims, saying the post had named certain constituencies and alleged that the ECI had counted zero votes there, but had not specified which records it was relying on.The Commission said Form 17C is the sole statutory account of votes cast at a polling station. It is prepared by the presiding officer at the close of polling.Copies of Part-I of Form 17C are given to polling agents appointed by candidates who are present at the polling station when voting concludes, the ECI said.On counting day, candidates' counting agents match the number of votes polled, recorded in Part-I of Form 17C, with the total number of votes counted, recorded in Part-II of the form.The Commission reiterated that all election-related data, including the number of votes polled and counted, had been made available through its statistical reports and index cards.It said the claims of discrepancies in the constituencies cited in the report were misleading and shared constituency-wise details to clarify the figures.
Article Summary: The Election Commission of India (ECI) rejected social media claims of discrepancies between the number of votes polled and votes counted in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. The Commission said it publishes details of electors, votes polled through electronic voting machines (EVMs), postal ballots and total votes cast.

Article Title: India must create, not just adopt inventions: Narayana Murthy calls for respect, better pay for teachers & researchers
Article Text:
Murthy said India had advanced in space, nuclear energy and vaccines but lagged in areas affecting everyday life.

BENGALURU: India must move beyond adopting inventions developed elsewhere and become a nation that creates them, Infosys founder NR Narayana Murthy said Thursday, stressing that this transition would require greater respect for teachers and researchers, better pay and sustained investment in education and research.In a recorded address at the Infosys Prize announcement in Bengaluru, Murthy argued that while India had made progress in areas such as space, atomic energy, vaccines and generic medicines, it continued to lag in several areas that directly affect citizens’ lives.The country needs to build a culture of innovation, backed by strong schools, better-trained teachers and researchers who are equipped and recognised for their work, he said.“A nation becomes economically powerful when it uses invention and continuous innovation to raise its per-capita income and improve the lives of its citizens. Invention and innovation are the two children of an inquiring mind, fortified by higher education and research,” he said.Murthy outlined four stages of economic development through invention and innovation. In the first, a nation neither invents nor innovates, and does not even use others’ ideas to improve its people’s lives.In the second, it adopts inventions and innovations made elsewhere without improving them. In the third, it uses higher education and research to improve existing ideas. The fourth is when a nation develops its own inventions.Assessing India’s position, he said its achievements in atomic energy, space, vaccines, the Green Revolution and generic medicines placed it in the second stage in most areas, while its Global Delivery Model represented the third. However, in making cities liveable, pollution-free and free of traffic congestion, and in providing clean, safe water, India remained at the first stage.He cited the US, western Europe, China and Japan as countries that had reached the fourth stage, and said India must aspire to do the same in every area affecting the lives of its poorest citizens, including those in remote villages.The transformation, he said, must begin in classrooms. Schools need to encourage independent, critical and analytical thinking, Socratic questioning and the ability to relate theory to the real world. While the National Education Policy (NEP) had started this journey, Murthy proposed a way to accelerate it by bringing in 10,000 accomplished retired science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) teachers from India and developed countries.They could run 2,500 'Train the Teacher' colleges across states and Union territories. Each team of four could train 100 primary and 100 secondary schoolteachers annually, taking the total to 5 lakh teachers a year. Within five years, those trained would themselves become trainers.Estimating the cost at about $100,000 per trainer a year, or $1 billion annually and $20 billion over 20 years, he said the investment was affordable for a country aspiring to become a $5-trillion economy. Invoking a line attributed to former Harvard president Derek Bok, he said: “If you think education is expensive, try ignorance.”But training alone would not suffice. “We must respect our teachers and researchers, pay them better, equip them well, and honour them. They are the role models for our young people,” he said.Murthy also recalled that Infosys instituted the Infosys Prize in 2009 to support research in India. Congratulating this year's laureates, he said the award was not a lifetime achievement recognition but was intended to spur them towards bigger work and greater honours.He urged India to cultivate global standards of productivity, discipline and hard work, while retaining the humility to learn from cultures that perform better.
Article Summary: Infosys founder NR Narayana Murthy said India had made progress in space, nuclear energy and vaccines but lagged in areas affecting everyday life. Murthy outlined four stages of economic development through invention and innovation. He said India must aspire to do the same in every area affecting the lives of its poorest citizens.

NEW DELHI: The next time you pick up a milk packet, a curd carton or a paneer pack, you may notice a new symbol on the label. From July 1, 2028, all milk and milk products, including composite milk products, will have to carry a distinctive, standardised blue-and-white droplet logo, providing a uniform identification mark for the category.The logo features a white droplet against a blue square background. FSSAI officials told TOI that the mark is intended to help consumers readily identify products in this category at the point of purchase, strengthen their awareness and understanding of the regulatory identity of milk and milk products, and facilitate quicker recognition of relevant information on product labels. It is also aimed at bringing greater consistency to labelling practices.The requirement has been notified through the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display) Second Amendment Regulations, 2026, published in the Gazette on November 9. The amendment to the 2020 labelling regulations will come into force on July 1, 2028.The authority has prescribed minimum dimensions for the logo according to the area of the package's principal display panel. The blue square must measure at least 6 mm on each side for panels up to 100 sq cm, 8 mm for panels measuring 100 to 500 sq cm, 12 mm for panels measuring 500 to 2,500 sq cm, and 16 mm for panels larger than 2,500 sq cm.The Gazette also specifies the minimum dimensions of the white droplet inside the square. For the smallest, 6 mm logo, the droplet must be at least 4.56 mm high and 3 mm wide. For the larger logo sizes, these dimensions increase to 6.08 mm by 4 mm, 9.12 mm by 6 mm and 12.16 mm by 8 mm, respectively.The amendment follows a draft proposal issued in February 2025, when FSSAI invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders. The authority said it considered the feedback received before finalising the regulations.
Article Summary: From July 1, 2028, all milk and milk products will have to carry a distinctive, standardised blue-and-white droplet logo. The logo features a white droplet against a blue square background. The mark is intended to help consumers readily identify products in this category at the point of purchase.

Article Title: India slips 5 spots on climate change performance index
Article Text:
The Bhagirathi Massif, a prominent mountain group is seen rising from the Gangotri Glacier in the Tapovan region of the Garhwal Himalaya range in the Indian state of Uttarakhand, on May 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Satish Sharma)

Energy use , GHG emissions led to India rank dip: Study authors

Changing trends

India has slipped five ranks down to 28th position on the Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI) 2027, released on Wednesday by prominent Germany-based environmental think tanks on the sidelines of the ongoing UN climate conference (COP31) and its leaders’ summit in Antalya, Turkiye.This is the third consecutive fall for India in the annual CCPI ranking. Significantly, the country was among the top 10 performers for six years in a row till 2024. India, which ranked 31st in 2014, entered the top 10 for the first time in 2019 and climbed as high as seventh rank, based on its high performance on the renewable energy front.CCPI, compiled by Germanwatch and NewClimate Institute, uses a standardised framework to compare the climate performance of 64 countries and EU as a whole, which, put together, account for over 90% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The performance of countries is assessed in four categories: GHG emissions (40%), renewable energy (20%), energy use (20%) and climate policy (20%).Responding to TOI’s question on the reason behind India’s fall in the rankings, the lead author of CCPI, Jan Burck, and co-author Madlen Peter said the country lost most ground in the energy use and GHG emissions categories. “India’s emissions and energy use per capita remain comparatively low, but both have risen in recent years.The CCPI rates both trends very low,” they said.The authors, however, appreciated India’s progress in expanding clean energy and recognised the challenge of meeting growing energy ne­eds across the country. “The rapid expansion of solar and wind power is a positive development. India’s renewable energy trend is rated high, although renewables still acco­unt for a relatively small sh­are of its overall energy su­p­p­ly.” The authors said India could use energy more effici­e­n­tly, invest in grids and storage to make better use of ren­e­w­able power and set a cl­e­ar ti­metable for reducing coal use to improve its performance.Denmark (ranked 4th) again topped CCPI, followed by Lithuania and Luxembourg (at 5th and 6th, respectively), with the top three ranks remaining vacant, as in previous years, in the absence of a perfect score for any country.On the other hand, the world’s largest emitter, China, is ranked 56th, whereas others in the league, Russia (66th), the US (67th) and Iran (68th), are the three worst performers in the overall rankings, with the report noting that none of the 65 largest emitters are on a Paris Agreement-compatible pathway.Pakistan, at 26th position, is ranked above India. It’s primarily due to comparatively lower GHG emissions in a relatively much smaller economy. The report also said the UK continues to be the only G20 country among the high per­formers. It said 10 G20 countries received an overall ‘very low’ rating, including twin COP presidencies Turkiye (53rd) and Australia (54th), even though G20 bears special responsibility for climate mitigation, as its members account for over 75% of global GHG emissions.
Article Summary: India has slipped five ranks down to 28th position on the Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI) 2027. This is the third consecutive fall for India in the annual CCPI ranking. Significantly, the country was among the top 10 performers for six years in a row till 2024.

Article Title: Pollution's hidden health cost: Dirty air may also raise diabetes risk, global review finds
Article Text:
Study analysed 13 earlier systematic reviews and meta-analyses on long-term PM2.5 exposure and diabetes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The damage caused by polluted air may not stop at the lungs. Long-term exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5), the tiny particles that can penetrate deep into the respiratory system, is also associated with a higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes. The risk was 10% to 16% higher for every 10 micrograms per cubic metre increase in PM2.5 exposure, according to a new global review, raising concerns about the wider health impact of air pollution.Published in the Journal of Vascular Diseases last month, the study analysed 13 earlier systematic reviews and meta-analyses on long-term PM2.5 exposure and diabetes. Six of the seven reviews examining new cases of type 2 diabetes found a 10% to 16% higher risk.The analysis covered studies from North America, Europe, East and South Asia, Latin America and Australia. A South Asian analysis involving populations in India, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka found a 9% higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes for every 10 micrograms per cubic metre increase in PM2.5 exposure.The review also linked PM2.5 exposure to diabetes prevalence, diabetes-related deaths and higher fasting blood glucose, but found no significant association with insulin resistance.Evidence on HbA1c, a measure of average blood sugar, was insufficient.The 13 reviews covered more than 200 million cumulative participant observations, not 200 million unique individuals, as some studies and populations overlapped. One review alone contributed about 198 million observations.The study was co-authored by Dr Anoop Misra, Executive Chairman and Director of Diabetes and Endocrinology at Fortis C-DOC Centre of Excellence for Diabetes, Metabolic Diseases and Endocrinology, New Delhi, along with Yashendra Sethi, Nirja Kaka, Saurabh Singhal, Manvi Vasudev and Giuseppe Biondi-Zoccai."Air quality management must become a core part of diabetes prevention," Misra said, stressing that air pollution should be viewed not only as an environmental and respiratory health concern but also as a factor in the broader cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic continuum.The researchers said possible mechanisms include inflammation, oxidative stress, impaired blood vessel function and disrupted insulin signalling, which may affect blood sugar regulation. However, these mechanisms were not systematically assessed. They cautioned that the findings show an association, not proof that pollution causes diabetes. Evidence for new cases was graded low, and the review did not establish whether cleaner air would reduce diabetes risk. They called for air quality to be considered in wider efforts to prevent cardiovascular, kidney and metabolic diseases.
Article Summary: Study analysed 13 earlier systematic reviews and meta-analyses on long-term PM2.5 exposure and diabetes. Six of the seven reviews examining new cases of type 2 diabetes found a 10% to 16% higher risk. Analysis covered studies from North America, Europe, East and South Asia, Latin America and Australia.

Article Title: Centre looks to open up car-rental market, cuts proposed minimum fleet to five
Article Text:
Centre looks to open up car-rental market, cuts proposed minimum fleet to five

NEW DELHI: In a move that could make it easier for more players to enter and expand in the self-drive and chauffeur-driven car rental business, the road transport ministry has proposed reducing the minimum fleet requirement to just five vehicles from the existing 50. The draft scheme also explicitly extends its coverage to rental vehicles offered with or without drivers.The road transport ministry has proposed sweeping changes in the draft Rent-a-Cab Scheme, 2026, which would be the first comprehensive replacement of the 1989 framework in 37 years. A limited amendment was carried out in 2021 by extending its coverage to battery-operated cabs and those running on methanol and ethanol that are exempt from permit requirements.The reduction in the minimum fleet requirement to just five vehicles -- a minimum of two vehicles stationed at each place of operation -- is likely to encourage smaller entrepreneurs, local car-rental companies and start-ups to enter the business. It may also help existing operators expand into more locations without having to maintain a large fleet.The proposed scheme, which ministry targets to roll out from next year also introduces stricter safety, insurance and operational requirements for companies renting out cars and at the same time it proposes to introduce online licencing, time-bound approvals and a formal grievance redressal mechanism.It proposes to fix the licencing fee at Rs 25,000, irrespective of the size of the fleet or the number of operating locations.The proposed framework also introduces a nine-year age limit for vehicles; valid registration, fitness and pollution certificates, paid motor vehicle tax and comprehensive insurance covering the renter, driver and other occupants up to the vehicle’s passenger capacity. Vehicles must also be free of specified pending challans and unpaid toll fees, and must not figure in the National Crime Records Bureau’s police crime database.Another major departure in the proposed scheme is it explicitly covers renting vehicles with or without drivers. The 1989 framework was primarily designed for self-drive rentals. Operators will now be required to provide drivers with valid licences, police-verified character and antecedents, no unpaid challans and welfare coverage under the Code on Social Security, 2020.The draft also introduces passenger-safety requirements, including vehicle location tracking devices, child restraint systems, first-aid kits and round-the-clock customer care. It proposes that operators must resolve website-based grievances within 24 hours and complete an inquiry into complaints against drivers within seven days.As per the draft, licencing will also become digital. Applications and renewals will be submitted electronically, with authorities required to process them within 60 days. The licence will remain valid for five years. Applications for adding or removing operating locations or vehicles will be deemed approved if authorities do not decide within 30 days.The new framework also proposes graded penalties for violations, including fines and suspension or cancellation of licences. These will be decided by state govts.The ministry has invited stakeholder comments on the draft until December 5.
Article Summary: The road transport ministry has proposed sweeping changes in the draft Rent-a- Cab Scheme, 2026. The proposed scheme would be the first comprehensive replacement of the 1989 framework in 37 years. The reduction in the minimum fleet requirement to just five vehicles is likely to encourage smaller entrepreneurs, local car-rental companies and start-ups.

Article Title: Yuge Yugeen museum set to open doors to public next year; cabinet approves Rs 3,230 cr
Article Text:
Yuge Yugeen museum set to open doors to public next year

NEW DELHI: North Block, which once housed the home and finance ministries, will reopen in less than a year from now, showcasing the first gallery of one of the largest museums in the world.Announced three years ago, Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum (YYBM) will be opened to public next year, govt said Wednesday after the cabinet committee on economic affairs (CCEA) cleared a Rs 3,230 crore development plan for the museum that will include the North and South Blocks and will be spread over nearly 1.8 lakh square metre, equal to 25 football fields. Once complete in 2031, the museum’s display area will be 1 lakh square metre, compared with 73,000 square metre of display area in Louvre and 70,000 square metre at the British Museum.On X, PM Narendra Modi said, “Imagine New Delhi becoming home to the world’s largest museum display area? Think scale. Think culture. That is the vision behind Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum...From ancient knowledge systems, mathematics and astronomy to architecture, art, languages and spirituality, the museum will bring thousands of years of our heritage to life through immersive experiences and world-class galleries.The project scheduled to be complete by March 2031 will cost nearly two-and-half times that of the new Parliament building.I&B minister Ashwini Vaishnaw told reporters that the museum aims at presenting the complete “civilisational journey” of India using modern technology while maintaining architectural integrity of the two buildings on Raisina Hill that were until recently the seat of power.Culture ministry, which is working on the project, was looking at opening the inaugural gallery by 2026-end.The ministry will soon start work on laying out the gallery, which will be on the theme of ‘adornment’ in the North Block, officials said. This gallery is expected to present the aesthetics that have defined India’s civilisational journey through the ages depicting it through the jewellery and decorations.A modular approach is being formulated to add more galleries. The content and collection analysis is being done and around 1.8 million objects have been identified from National Museum and other culture ministry museums, 52 Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) site museums and various state museums and private collections to be displayed in the YYBM.Although the museum will open next year, the metro station that will come up next to Rakabganj Gurdwara is likely to be operational by June 2029 and will act as a crucial link given that nearly 70% of visitors are expected to come from the entry gate behind the North Block. The earlier plan to explore connecting the North and South Blocks through an underground tunnel has been dropped and will now have a surface level connection, officials said.The museum is also expected to generate recurring revenue through ticket sales, food and beverage facilities, events and venue rentals, digital experiences, guided tours, retail outlets and other visitor services.TOI has learnt that the CCEA has approved the culture ministry’s proposal of annual revenue generation of around Rs 163 crore from letting out five auditoriums and venues for events and programmes, seven food courts and sale of tickets.The ministry, in its proposal, has proposed Rs 100 as ticket for Indians and Rs 1,000 for foreigners.Considering the scale of the museum, there will be a separate director general and four additional director generals for the project. People aware of the project said around 262 posts would be created, including curators and support staff.
Article Summary: Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum (YYBM) will be opened to public next year, govt said. The museum will include the North and South Blocks and will be spread over nearly 1.8 lakh square metre, equal to 25 football fields. Once complete in 2031, the museum’s display area will be 1 lakh square metres, compared with 73,000 square metre of display area in Louvre.

NEW DELHI: In a move that could spare lakhs of students long journeys for entrance examinations, the education ministry has initiated an exercise to create a nationwide pool of standardised examination centres, with the aim of having at least one in every district. Article Title: Watch: Tamil Nadu CM Vijay launches one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns
Article Text:
Vijay presented 22-carat, one-gram gold rings to 25 newborns. (PTI)

Who is eligible for the gold ring?

Scheme draws on Tamil tradition

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. He also held some of the newborns and presented the rings to beneficiaries during the launch programme.Under the scheme, eligible babies born in government hospitals and government primary health centres will receive a 22-carat, one-gram gold ring.The initiative, named the Maternal Uncle Gold Ring Scheme (Thaaimaman Thanga Mothiram Thittam), has an annual allocation of Rs 755.83 crore.It is aimed at celebrating motherhood, promoting maternal and child health and encouraging institutional deliveries by increasing public confidence in government healthcare facilities.The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions.Mothers must be registered under the Pregnancy and Infant Cohort Monitoring and Evaluation (PICME) system and have a Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) ID. They will also have to provide an e-KYC-verified Aadhaar card along with one of the prescribed identity or residence documents.These include ration cards, voter identity cards, Labour Welfare Board identity cards, Department of Posts address cards and nativity certificates.The state government has already procured 1.28 lakh one-gram gold rings for the initial rollout. Each ring will have a unique serial number and will be packed in tamper-proof packaging.From Monday, babies born in government hospitals will receive the rings at the time of discharge, according to the state government.To clear the backlog of eligible babies born between June 22 and Monday, the government will distribute the rings through 107 hubs across Tamil Nadu.Distribution will begin at the rate of 100 babies per day at each hub. At designated centres, 25 beneficiaries will be accommodated in the morning and another 25 in the afternoon to avoid overcrowding, PTI reported.Village Health Nurses will distribute invitations informing beneficiaries of their allotted date and time. Beneficiaries have been asked to visit the designated centres only at the time mentioned in their invitations.The district administration has also made transportation arrangements for beneficiaries from their respective areas. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election as a symbolic gift to newborns, drawing on the Tamil tradition of ‘Thaimaaman Seer’. The scheme has retrospective effect from June 22, Vijay’s birthday.A government order issued on June 23 described the initiative as a token celebrating the birth of a child, motherhood and the cultural tradition of ‘Thaimaaman’.According to ANI, Tamil Nadu minister Arun Raj explained the cultural significance of the initiative saying, "A maternal uncle is someone who is among the first to rush in when a child is born, sharing in his sister’s happiness as his own. He assures her that he will always stand by her and her child, offering love, support and a sense of security.""Today, the Tamil Nadu Government, under the leadership of our brother, Mr. Vijay, is embracing this sacred bond of the maternal uncle and, as a gesture of that affection, is set to provide a one-gram gold ring to every child born in government hospitals. When the scheme was announced and the question arose as to where it should be launched, the place chosen by our Chief Minister was Madurai. This is the sacred soil of Madurai, blessed with the compassion and grace of Mother Meenakshi," he added.Tamil Nadu records around 7.8 lakh deliveries annually, with institutional deliveries accounting for 99.9% of births, according to NFHS-6. Government health facilities account for nearly 4.2 lakh deliveries, or around 53% of the total.According to the state government, the average out-of-pocket expenditure for a delivery at a government hospital is Rs 1,364, compared with Rs 63,473 at a private hospital.The government said the scheme is intended to encourage safe institutional deliveries, strengthen maternal and child welfare and increase public trust in government healthcare services.The Tamil Nadu Medical Services Corporation will procure the gold rings based on annual requirements, while a project and programme management unit will oversee implementation and monitoring.
Article Summary: Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay on Monday rolled out the state government’s one-gram gold ring scheme for newborns in Madurai. The scheme will cover babies born on or after June 22, 2026, to mothers who are permanent residents of Tamil Nadu and have delivered at government healthcare institutions. Vijay had announced the scheme ahead of the April 23 Assembly election.
