Nvidia's most likely move is Kress now and a longer search after

Nvidia has never had to think seriously about who comes after Jensen Huang. He co-founded the company in 1993, has been its only chief executive since, and built it so completely around himself that succession always felt like a question for some distant year. That year may have arrived this week.On November 8, the chipmaker's board opened an independent investigation following reports that Huang, 63, had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. The New York Times had reported on October 29 that Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, sought to cultivate close ties with him, and both the Times and the Financial Times reported that US intelligence agencies suspect she was passing information to Beijing. In an email to staff on November 8, Huang admitted to the affair. China has dismissed the allegations as a smear. The board said it still had confidence in him, and on November 10 it hired Joon H. Kim, a former acting US attorney for the Southern District of New York, at law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the probe.By November 11, the mood had turned. The New York Times reported that Huang had also been in a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare and one of his direct reports.Minutes later, The Wall Street Journal reported that the board was preparing to force him out. Directors met late into the night, shares fell more than 9% in after-hours trading, and Bloomberg reported that the board is working with an outside firm to explore replacements. At the time of writing, the company has not announced a decision.Under the company's bylaws, a majority of directors can replace the CEO without cause. The harder part is finding the name that goes in his place.Jensen Huang runs one of the flattest structures in big tech. He had 55 direct reports in 2024 and 36 by late 2025, and he skips one-on-one meetings so that every leader hears the same thing at the same time. Asked about succession, he has said there will "never be one like me," while arguing that the dozens of executives around him could each run a company of their own because they have watched him make every decision.That design kept Nvidia fast. It also means nobody below Huang has ever held a view of the whole company. The bench got thinner in August, when Jay Puri, who ran worldwide sales for two decades, retired and handed over to former Microsoft executive Nick Parker.These are the seven names now in the frame, two of them from Huang's own family.Kress has been chief financial officer since 2013. Before that she was CFO of Cisco's business technology and operations finance organisation, and spent 13 years at Microsoft, the last four as CFO of its Server and Tools division, after starting out in finance at Texas Instruments. After Huang, she is the executive investors know best, the voice that has walked Wall Street through every quarter of the AI boom, including a fiscal 2026 in which revenue grew 65% to $215.9 billion. Semafor reported that some directors favour naming her interim CEO.The doubt is about what comes after. Her entire career has been in finance, and analysts do not see her as a natural successor to Huang's role as the company's technology visionary. As a stabiliser while the board searches, though, no one else is as ready. She already owns the numbers the market is holding the company to, including her own forecast of 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028.Buck created CUDA, the software platform that made Nvidia's GPUs the default choice for AI work and that rivals still struggle to match. The idea began at Stanford, where his PhD work produced Brook, an early attempt at running general-purpose code on graphics chips, and Nvidia hired him in 2004 to turn it into a product. In roughly 22 years at the company, he has risen to run hyperscale and high-performance computing, the heart of the data centre business that now brings in most of its revenue. His job puts him in daily contact with Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta and OpenAI.Bettors on Polymarket have him as favourite for the permanent role. He also brings something this moment needs, having testified before the US Congress on AI and advised the White House. Some analysts have floated a shared interim arrangement, with Kress handling the finances and Buck the technology and customer relationships. The open question is whether a product leader who has never run the whole company can carry its public face the way Huang did.Haas has been CEO of Arm since 2022, but before that he spent seven years at Nvidia, rising to run its computing products business. He took Arm public in 2023, and in March he moved it beyond licensing designs to selling its own chip for the first time, a data centre processor called the AGI CPU, with Meta as its first customer. Few outsiders combine first-hand knowledge of how Huang operates with experience steering a listed chip company through that kind of change.Futurum Group analyst Shay Boloor wrote on X that if he had to bet on an external pick, it would be Haas. Polymarket odds on him have since dropped sharply, and the timing works against him. Having just put Arm into competition with some of its own customers, Nvidia among them, he would be walking away from the biggest bet of his tenure.Srouji led Apple's in-house silicon programme from its first chip, the A4, in 2008, through to the processors that now power every iPhone and Mac, and his group went on to take over batteries, cameras, displays and Apple's own cellular modems. Before Apple, he worked on processor design at Intel and IBM. In April, Apple made him chief hardware officer, placing its entire hardware engineering organisation under him as John Ternus prepared to take over from Tim Cook.His name has come up as a possible external successor. On paper, he offers what Kress cannot: an engineer who built a chip team from scratch inside a company that had never designed its own processors. The difficulty is timing. He has only just been handed the largest role of his career in Cupertino, which would make him hard to lure away.The former Google CEO is the least conventional name here, and he already has a job: since March 2025 he has been CEO and controlling shareholder of rocket maker Relativity Space. Still, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of the Yale School of Management, who advises chief executives and boards, has said he has heard Schmidt rumoured as a possible choice and that Schmidt "could step in tomorrow and do a very good job."Schmidt ran Google from 2001 to 2011, taking it from a fast-growing search company to a global giant, and has since spent years on AI and national security policy in Washington. That last part matters now. A board dealing with a spy investigation, congressional pressure and nervous shareholders may value a calm, well-connected figure more than an engineer, at least for a while.Jensen Huang's daughter took a route into technology unlike anyone else on this list. She trained at The Culinary Institute of America and Le Cordon Bleu, cooked in restaurant kitchens, then spent close to four years at LVMH marketing champagne brands such as Dom Pérignon and Veuve Clicquot. In 2019 she started an MBA at London Business School and took a short AI course at MIT, and in 2020 she joined Nvidia as a marketing intern. She is now senior director of product and technical marketing for the company's physical AI platforms, including Omniverse, Cosmos and Isaac.Her growing number of public appearances with her father, including at the World Robot Conference in Beijing in August, has fed talk that she is being prepared for more, and former employees have said her influence reaches beyond her formal marketing role. Still, Nvidia's 2026 proxy filing shows she is not an executive officer and does not report directly to her father. Huang has said his children would have to earn the top job, and a jump from senior director to CEO would be a hard sell to shareholders already rattled by this week.Caprez, 35, is a former Swiss national team ski racer who studied banking and finance at the University of Zurich and worked as a consultant at BCG before meeting Madison as a classmate at London Business School. He joined Nvidia in early 2024 as a corporate development manager, recruited with her help, and became vice president of global AI infrastructure growth in January. The two married in Hawaii in September.The Information, which spoke to more than a dozen people who work with him, described Caprez as Huang's "consigliere" and the company's main contact for neoclouds, the newer cloud providers that rent out Nvidia GPUs. Brookfield's Sikander Rashid has recalled Huang telling him that if he wanted something done, he should talk to Nico. One colleague told the publication they imagined Huang was preparing Madison and Caprez for the next step. Less than three years at the company, though, would make his case harder to defend than anyone else's here.Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy has compared the moment to Intel's 2018 removal of Brian Krzanich over a relationship with an employee, while noting that the chip plans are set years ahead, so the near-term risk to the business is limited. D.A. Davidson's Gil Luria was blunter, warning that the episode could force a transition the company is not prepared for. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney went the other way, saying that removing Huang would be as foolish as Apple's firing of Steve Jobs.If the board does move, the first name announced is most likely to be Kress. Reports that directors favour her as interim CEO, her 13 years as the company's public financial voice and the board's need to steady investors all point the same way. The permanent job will take a longer search, and on current signals Buck is the insider best placed for it, possibly after a spell sharing the interim role with Kress. Huang always argued that Nvidia did not need a formal succession plan because everyone around him had seen how he thinks. The board is about to find out whether he was right.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, has been its only chief executive since. Colette Kress is the safest pair of hands for the interim job. Ian Buck has the strongest claim among the engineers. Rene Haas is the outsider who already knows the culture. Johny Srouji would bring Apple's chip discipline. Eric Schmidt is the caretaker some would reach for.

Article Title: Term insurance explained: How it differs from other life insurance plans
Article Text:
Term insurance is considered the purest form of life insurance.

By Sabvir Singh

What exactly is term insurance?

How do other life insurance plans differ?

Endowment plans

Participating, or par,

Non-participating plans

Money-back plans

Unit-linked insurance plans (ULIPs)

Pension ULIPs

Annuity plans

Why does the amount of cover matter?

The bottom line

(The author is Joint Group CEO, PB Fintech)

While there is growing awareness about the importance of life insurance, choosing the right policy can be less straightforward. The market offers several products, from term insurance and endowment plans to money-back policies and unit-linked insurance plans (ULIPs). While all fall under the life insurance umbrella, they differ in the benefits they offer and the financial needs they are designed to meet.Term insurance is considered the purest form of life insurance, as its primary purpose is to provide financial protection to dependants in the event of the policyholder's death. It offers substantial life cover at a relatively affordable premium. For instance, a healthy 30-year-old male may be able to secure Rs 1 crore of cover for less than Rs 1,000 a month, depending on the insurer, policy term and other factors.Life insurance needs can also evolve at different stages of life. While someone early in their career may prioritise financial protection, a person with growing family responsibilities may look at higher life cover. Savings-linked policies or annuity products may become relevant for those looking to build savings or secure a regular retirement income. Understanding how these products differ can help buyers choose according to their changing needs.Term insurance provides life cover for a specified period. You pay a premium to keep the policy active, and if you die during the policy term, the insurer pays the death benefit to your nominee.For a family with a home loan, a young child and regular household expenses, this payout can help replace the income lost when the primary earner dies. The money can be used to repay outstanding loans, fund a child's education or meet everyday expenses.Term plans also come with a special exit option which allows policyholder to get back 100% of the premiums paid at a specified age (generally near retirement). This gives a lifetime of protection and option to get back premiums paid when they feel their financial dependencies are over.Premiums are generally lower at younger ages, although health, lifestyle, policy duration and underwriting conditions also affect pricing and eligibility.Life insurance includes products designed to meet different needs. While term insurance focuses primarily on financial protection, other plans may combine life cover with savings, market-linked investments or retirement income.combine life cover with a savings component. There are usually 2 types of endowment plans: Participating and Non-Participating. Depending on the policy, the policyholder may receive a maturity benefit on surviving the term, while the nominee may receive a death benefit if the policyholder dies during the term.plans allow eligible policyholders to receive bonuses linked to the surplus of the insurer's participating fund, in addition to the benefits specified in the policy. Future bonuses are generally not guaranteed until declared.do not share in the insurer's surplus but provide maturity benefit which is 100% guaranteedprovide periodic payouts during the policy term, as specified in the contract. They can suit people who prefer to receive a portion of their policy benefits at predetermined intervals rather than wait until maturity. However, similar to endowment plans the customer can choose between non-participating and participating.Both endowment and money-back plans are non-market linked planscombine life cover with investments in market-linked funds. The premium is invested in funds such as equity, debt or balanced funds based on your financial goals and risk appetite. The investment value depends on market performance, and returns are not guaranteed.combine market-linked wealth creation with retirement planning, helping individuals build a retirement corpus during their working years. They offer a choice of equity, debt or balanced funds to suit individual financial goals and risk appetite. At maturity, up to 60% of the corpus can be withdrawn tax-free, subject to applicable tax provisions, while at least 40% must be used to purchase an annuity that provides a guaranteed income for life.are designed to provide a regular income, often during retirement. An immediate annuity can begin paying income soon after purchase, while a deferred annuity starts payments at a later date. Depending on the option selected, payouts may continue for the policyholder's lifetime or include benefits for a surviving spouse.Each product has a different structure. The right choice depends on whether the buyer's priority is financial protection, a combination of protection and savings, market-linked investment or income during retirement.One important consideration when comparing policies is how much life cover they provide relative to the premium.Since a pure term plan does not provide a maturity benefit, it can generally offer a larger sum assured for the same premium than a savings-linked policy. Savings-linked plans, meanwhile, are structured to provide additional benefits, depending on the product.A common starting point for estimating term life cover is 10 to 15 times annual income. This is only a rule of thumb. Outstanding loans, future education expenses, existing savings, the number of dependents and other household income should also inform the calculation.Term insurance is one type of life insurance, designed primarily to protect dependents against the financial consequences of the policyholder's death. Other life insurance products may combine protection with savings, investments or retirement income.Understanding these differences helps buyers choose products that match their needs at different stages of life. Whether the priority is protecting a young family, building savings or planning for retirement, the starting point is to understand what each policy offers and how it fits into the wider financial plan.
Article Summary: Life insurance includes products designed to meet different needs. Term insurance is considered the purest form of life insurance. Other plans may combine life cover with savings, market-linked investments or retirement income. The right choice depends on whether different product has a different structure.
